```{=html}
<div class="project-intro">

  <div class="project-image">
    <img src="../images/AUV.JPEG" alt="Final autonomous ocean profiling robot">
    <div class="project-caption">A picture of our final robot build.</div>
  </div>

  <div class="project-text">
    <p>All spring semester sophomore engineers at Harvey Mudd undergo a rigorous lab-based class called E80, or Experimental Engineering. In the latter half of this class, students work in teams to develop a fully autonomous underwater robot that measures a phenomenon of their choice with a limit of $50 to purchase sensors. At the end of the class, the robot is deployed at Dana Point Beach, a harbor in the suburbs of Los Angeles.</p>

    <p>Our team chose to measure pressure, temperature, and ultraviolet light intensity as a function of depth in marine environments — phenomena directly tied to ocean health and climate monitoring. With a tight budget and real deployment conditions, every engineering decision carried weight.</p>

    <p>I led the electrical system design, implementing 3 analog circuits with three unique electrical interfaces: voltage-to-voltage, current-to-voltage, and resistance-to-voltage. Each sensor system — UV, pressure, and temperature — was engineered using a unity-gain buffer and inverting gain amplifier to tailor sensor output to a specific range, enhancing data resolution and preventing data clipping on the Teensy 4.0.</p>

    <p>Calibration was one of the most technically demanding aspects of the project. I developed protocols that accounted for noise, sensor non-linearity, and degradation — ensuring robust and accurate measurements across diverse underwater conditions. On the mechanical side, I helped design and fabricate a system that maintained neutral buoyancy in saltwater while minimizing axial tilt, improving stability during data collection.</p>
  </div>

</div>

<p>To control the robot autonomously, I developed a C++ algorithm for dynamic depth control, enabling the robot to reach and maintain designated waypoints at various depths. Once the data was collected, I developed MATLAB scripts to process the output and generate clear, interpretable graphs of temperature and UV intensity as a function of depth — aiding data analysis and decision-making for climate monitoring.</p>
```
